# Contracts for small in-memory pipelines

[← All question groups](../index.md) · `dotnet-collections-delegates` · **C# & .NET Runtime** · Catalog level: foundation

<p>Questions come from the preserved source notes. Reframing, assessment intent, senior signals and rubrics are editorial interpretations, not verified model answers or universal interviewer expectations. Follow-ups and the combined production exercise are agent additions. Reading this bank creates no learning record, score, completion or review schedule.</p>

## Start with one representative question

[S01-Q021](#S01-Q021)

<p>Which collections would you choose for common work such as ordered processing, keyed lookup or duplicate detection? Explain one choice in depth.</p>

## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Choose data and callback contracts that make a small processing pipeline correct and understandable.</p>

<ul>
<li>Select enumeration, indexing or mutation from caller requirements.</li>
<li>Define equality and duplicate handling for keyed or set-based operations.</li>
<li>Choose text-building and callback signatures without unsupported cost claims.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

No catalog prerequisite. Establish the terms and scenario assumptions in the foundation questions before progressing; a published lesson is not evidence that you know them.

<p>The questions move from how data is exposed to how it is looked up, transformed and turned into text. Collections, delegates and strings belong to that processing flow, but each choice must answer a specific contract rather than share a universal “fastest” rule.</p>

<a id="S01-Q002"></a>

### S01-Q002 · Foundation

<p>How would you compare an empty string literal with String.Empty in ordinary C# code? Which differences actually matter to the caller?</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q002](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q002)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q002](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q002)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What is the difference between an empty string literal and `String.Empty`?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Separate representation, readable intent and observable string behavior. Avoid treating a stylistic preference as a performance measurement.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Distinguish semantic requirements from unsupported micro-optimization claims.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Compare non-null empty strings, not null or whitespace; name the runtime and workload before discussing measured cost.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Checks equality and relevant API contracts with a minimal example.</li>
<li>States which style choice is conventional and which performance claim needs evidence.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Confusing empty with null, or promising that one spelling is always faster.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would your validation change if null and whitespace were also allowed?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q009"></a>

### S01-Q009 · Foundation

<p>Compare IEnumerable, arrays, IList and List for a caller that needs to read or modify a collection. What contract would you expose?</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q009](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q009)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q009](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q009)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Compare `IEnumerable`, arrays, `IList`, and `List`.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Separate an interface’s promises from a concrete collection’s behavior. Explain which operations the caller needs instead of ranking every collection together.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Choose a collection contract from access and mutation requirements.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State generic or non-generic forms and whether size, indexing and mutation are required; distinguish the exposed contract from the backing implementation.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Maps required operations to a suitable contract and tests its limitations.</li>
<li>Explains what consumers may assume without depending on one concrete implementation.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Treating enumeration as proof that the collection is mutable, indexed or already materialized.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What changes when consumers must not alter the collection?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q023"></a>

### S01-Q023 · Mechanism

<p>Explain delegates, Action, Func and Predicate through a callback contract. How would you choose a signature that expresses what the caller expects?</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q023](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q023)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q023](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q023)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain delegates, `Action`, `Func`, and `Predicate`.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>A callback is behavior supplied to be invoked by another operation. Compare inputs, outputs and intent instead of only reciting generic parameter counts.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Express a behavior boundary with a clear callable contract.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use a synchronous callback first; state separately whether closures, multiple handlers or asynchronous returns are part of the example.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Explains the chosen inputs and return contract using a concrete invocation.</li>
<li>Discusses an exception or captured-state boundary and how the caller handles it.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Naming delegate types without explaining the behavior supplied or the result expected.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What would change if the callback needed to perform asynchronous work?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q021"></a>

### S01-Q021 · Application

<p>Which collections would you choose for common work such as ordered processing, keyed lookup or duplicate detection? Explain one choice in depth.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q021](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q021)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q021](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q021)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What collections do you commonly use and why?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Connect an actual access pattern to a collection contract. The source asks about familiarity; a truthful example or a clearly hypothetical design is sufficient.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Defend a collection choice with correctness and cost requirements.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State ordering, duplicates, mutation and expected input size; distinguish personal use from a proposed example rather than inventing experience.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Explains the required operations and a condition that changes the choice.</li>
<li>Checks correctness before presenting complexity assumptions or measured resource costs.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Listing collection names or claiming one is best for all access patterns.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>Which requirement would make your chosen collection unsuitable?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q019"></a>

### S01-Q019 · Trade-offs

<p>When would you choose string operations or StringBuilder to construct text? Explain how the workload would influence your choice.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q019](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q019)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q019](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q019)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Compare `string` and `StringBuilder`.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Relate the text-building pattern to the work performed rather than recommending one API universally. State what evidence could justify an optimization.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Choose a text-building strategy from actual workload characteristics.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Specify input size, number of appends and runtime before comparing measured cost; include a simple case as well as repeated construction.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Explains the relevant construction mechanism and predicts where cost may accumulate.</li>
<li>Proposes a representative measurement while considering readability and allocation.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Claiming StringBuilder is always faster without considering the size or construction pattern.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What would your benchmark need to prevent a misleading comparison?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q022"></a>

### S01-Q022 · Trade-offs

<p>When would you use Dictionary and when would you use HashSet? Describe the contract for keys or members before comparing their costs.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q022](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q022)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q022](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q022)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> When would you choose `Dictionary` or `HashSet`?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Choose based on whether the operation needs associated values, membership or uniqueness. Make the application’s definition of duplicate explicit.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Select a keyed or set-based collection for a stated operation.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Specify equality rules, duplicates, input scale and mutation; cost claims need appropriate implementation and workload assumptions.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Demonstrates the required lookup or duplicate-handling behavior on a small input.</li>
<li>Explains equality consistency and when a different collection would fit better.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Choosing solely from a memorized constant-time claim without specifying the operation or equality contract.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would case-insensitive string input change your requirements?</li>
</ul>

</details>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>A hypothetical component filters submitted identifiers, removes duplicates and builds a report through a supplied callback. Define ordering, mutation, string emptiness and callback results. Select collections and text construction, test empty and duplicate inputs, and propose a representative cost measurement.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Selects contracts that satisfy the requested operations and boundary inputs.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Explains equality, callback failure and cost assumptions, then compares a relevant alternative.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>Naming APIs or quoting complexity alone does not prove this pipeline’s correctness or cost.</p>
